parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State **two** advantages of the transmission of data in digital, rather than analogue, form.

markscheme_points.text: any two points from:; signal can be regenerated / noise can be removed; signal can be encrypted; signal can be checked for errors; multiplexing is possible; circuits are more reliable / cheaper; data can be transmitted at a greater rate

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to unwanted extra signal (noise) as it travels along a wire - how does a digital receiver decide if a pulse is a 0 or a 1 compared to an analogue receiver?
Hint 2: Think of two extra processing tricks that only work easily with numbers - checking for mistakes, scrambling for security, or sending many conversations together.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: signal can be regenerated and noise removed; signal can be encrypted for security; error detection / correction can be applied; time-division multiplexing is possible; higher data transmission rate; digital circuits are cheaper / more reliable.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why digital copes better with noise**
Think of analogue as a smooth varying voltage where every tiny change matters. Any noise picked up adds on and cannot be separated. Digital is just high or low, 1 or 0. A regenerator only needs to decide which one it was, remake a clean new pulse, and the noise is gone.

Step 2: **Why numbers are easier to process**
Once your sound is just a string of binary numbers you can do maths on it. You can add extra parity bits to check for errors, encrypt it with a code, interleave many signals by multiplexing, and send it very fast using processors. Pick any two of these distinct advantages for your two lines.

parts.part_stem:
The transmission system may be represented in block form as in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

The variation with time $t$ of part of the input analogue signal is shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2

The analogue signal is sampled at time intervals of $0.10\text{ ms}$. The first sample is taken at time $t = 0$.

Some values of the sampled analogue signal and the corresponding digital signals are shown in Table 4.1.

Each digitised number contains four bits.

Table 4.1
parts.text: An analogue signal is to be transmitted in digital form.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: In Table 4.1, underline the least significant bit (LSB) in the digital signal for the time of $0.20\text{ ms}$.
hints: Hint 1: Write the 4-bit number 0110 as place values 8-4-2-1 from left to right and ask which end changes the total by only 1 if it flips.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Most versus least significant**
In a 4-bit number the columns from the left are $$8 \; 4 \; 2 \; 1$$ So for $0110$: $$0 \times 8 + 1 \times 4 + 1 \times 2 + 0 \times 1 = 6$$ The left-most bit changes the value by 8, the right-most bit changes it by only 1. That right-most bit is the least significant bit (LSB), so underline the final 0.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.2 and read straight up from $t = 0.30$, $0.40$ and $0.50$ ms to the curve, then across to the mV axis to get the three sampled analogue voltages.
Hint 2: Look at the pattern already given: $5.7$ mV becomes 0101 (=5) and $6.2$ mV becomes 0110 (=6) - what rounding rule to a whole number is being used?
Hint 3: Convert each new whole number to 4-bit binary using 8-4-2-1 columns, remembering to keep leading zeros to make four bits.
parts.proper_answer: Analogue samples: $3.0\text{ mV}$ at $0.30\text{ ms}$, $4.8\text{ mV}$ at $0.40\text{ ms}$, $1.0\text{ mV}$ at $0.50\text{ ms}$. Digital signals: 0011 at $0.30\text{ ms}$, 0100 at $0.40\text{ ms}$, 0001 at $0.50\text{ ms}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sample the graph**
Sampling means measuring the smooth curve at fixed times. Read vertically up from the $t$-axis to the curve in Fig. 4.2. You get about $$V(0.30) \approx 3.0\text{ mV}$$ $$V(0.40) \approx 4.8\text{ mV}$$ $$V(0.50) \approx 1.0\text{ mV}$$

Step 2: **See how the ADC rounds**
The table shows $5.7$ goes to $0101 = 5$ and $6.2$ goes to $0110 = 6$. So it takes the integer part (rounds down to the nearest whole mV). Apply the same: $3.0$ to $3$, $4.8$ to $4$, $1.0$ to $1$.

Step 3: **Code to 4-bit binary**
Use columns $8$-$4$-$2$-$1$: $$3 = 0\times8+0\times4+1\times2+1\times1 = 0011$$ $$4 = 0\times8+1\times4+0\times2+0\times1 = 0100$$ $$1 = 0\times8+0\times4+0\times2+1\times1 = 0001$$ Enter these under $0.30$, $0.40$ and $0.50$ ms respectively.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
A single bit from the output of the digital-to-analogue converter corresponds to an output analogue signal of $1.0\text{ mV}$.

Assume that the conversion and transmission do not introduce a time delay.

On the axes of Fig. 4.3, show the variation with time $t$ of the output from the digital-to-analogue converter.

{{figure:figure_4_3}}

Fig. 4.3

markscheme_points.text: series of steps, all of width 0.1 ms
steps levels, in order, at output voltage 0, 5, 6, 3
markscheme_points.guidance: 2 marks: all levels correct; 1 mark: one level incorrect and all others correct

hints: Hint 1: Start from your digital numbers in Table 4.1 - what decimal value 0 to 15 does each 4-bit code represent, and with $1.0$ mV per bit what output voltage does that give?
Hint 2: Remember a DAC holds each value constant until the next sample arrives - what shape does that make on a voltage-time graph if samples are $0.10$ ms apart?
Hint 3: Check the start and end times: from $t=0$ to $0.10$ ms the output stays at the first value, then jumps vertically at each sampling instant with no time delay.
parts.proper_answer: Staircase of horizontal steps of width $0.10\text{ ms}$. Output levels in order: $0\text{ mV}$, $5\text{ mV}$, $6\text{ mV}$, $3\text{ mV}$, $4\text{ mV}$, $1\text{ mV}$, each held constant until the next sample time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert bits back to volts**
One LSB = $1.0\text{ mV}$, so output voltage = binary value in decimal $\times 1.0\text{ mV}$. From part (b): $$0000 = 0 \to 0\text{ mV}$$ $$0101 = 5 \to 5\text{ mV}$$ $$0110 = 6 \to 6\text{ mV}$$ $$0011 = 3 \to 3\text{ mV}$$ $$0100 = 4 \to 4\text{ mV}$$ $$0001 = 1 \to 1\text{ mV}$$

Step 2: **Draw the hold shape**
The DAC cannot follow the smooth original. It outputs a constant voltage then jumps suddenly at the next sample. So draw horizontal lines: $0$ mV from $0$ to $0.10$ ms, $5$ mV from $0.10$ to $0.20$ ms, $6$ mV from $0.20$ to $0.30$ ms, and so on, with vertical jumps at $0.10$, $0.20$, $0.30$, $0.40$ ms.

Step 3: **Finish the staircase**
Continue with $3$ mV from $0.30$ to $0.40$ ms, $4$ mV from $0.40$ to $0.50$ ms, ending at $1$ mV at $0.50$ ms. This stepped, blocky version is the reconstructed analogue signal - close to Fig. 4.2 but with quantisation steps.
